blocks.text: Romans 3 begins by affirming Jewish advantage, especially the entrusting of God's oracles, while insisting that God's faithfulness is not cancelled by human unfaithfulness. Paul then places Jews and Greeks alike under sin, using a sequence of scriptural accusations. He turns to God's righteousness manifested apart from the law and speaks of faith, grace, redemption, justification, and atoning or mercy-seat imagery in Christ. The chapter excludes boasting, asks whether God is God of Jews only, and concludes that faith does not overthrow the law.

sections.title: God's righteousness and humanity under sin

blocks.text: The supplied context describes ancient courts as issuing verdicts that established status, and Scripture uses that legal language for God's saving declaration. Romans 3 uses this courtroom vocabulary while also joining it to covenant, faith, grace, redemption, and God's judgment, so justification should not be reduced to a contextless legal slogan.

Several key expressions in Romans 3 remain contested. Dikaiosyne theou can gather God's saving justice, covenant faithfulness, rectitude, or a status-giving verdict. Pistis Christou can be read as faith in Christ, Christ's faithfulness, or a deliberately dense relation. Erga nomou can refer to works of law or Torah without licensing a caricature of Judaism as simple legalism. Hilasterion may evoke atonement, expiation, propitiation, or the mercy seat; the uncertainty should be preserved rather than hidden by a single gloss.

sections.title: Terms that carry more than one reading

blocks.text: Romans 3 preserves Jewish advantage—the entrusted oracles—while arguing that Jews and Greeks alike are under sin. It then excludes boasting and asks whether the one God is God of Jews only or also of Gentiles. The chapter's universal accountability therefore does not erase Jewish scriptural vocation, and its shared access to justification does not become ethnic triumphalism.

sections.title: One God and the exclusion of boasting
